title: Windows: replace sysinfo with PDH backend for frequency_series
description:
On Windows, sysinfo's per-core frequency API returns the **nominal/base** frequency rather than the actual running frequency. Verified with envelope nuc13-002_20260526_113054.json from an i5-1340P NUC: 61 samples over a 60s sustained-load run, every sample identical at [1900*8 P-cores, 1400*8 E-cores], mean_mhz constant at 1650 throughout. This makes frequency_series useless on Windows for its primary purpose (detecting thermal throttling).

Iteration-time drift on the same run showed ~33% slowdown (3ms → 4ms median), so we have *a* signal but it's coarse and not directly comparable to prime95 evidence. Mark's StressCPU.ps1 uses real freq counters and that's the bar we need to match.

## Approach

Use Performance Data Helper (PDH) counters instead of sysinfo on Windows. The right counter is:

  \Processor Information(*)\% Processor Performance

This returns actual frequency as a percentage of nominal (100 = at base, 200 = boosting to 2x base, 79 = throttled to ~80%). Multiply by the per-core nominal base frequency (which sysinfo already exposes correctly via CpuInfo.frequency_mhz, or PDH's \Processor Information(_Total)\Processor Frequency) to get actual MHz.

Note: '\Processor Information(*)\Processor Frequency' returns the **base** frequency, not actual. That's the trap sysinfo fell into. Do not use it.

## Implementation notes

- New file collector/src/freq_windows.rs with a PDH-based Sampler.
- cfg-gate so non-Windows builds are unaffected. freq_sampler.rs dispatches.
- Add windows-sys as a windows-only dep: features = ["Win32_System_Performance", "Win32_Foundation"].
- PDH percentage counters need a delta: first PdhCollectQueryData returns garbage; collect twice (or wait one interval) before recording the first real sample.
- Stop semantics: PdhCloseQuery in Sampler::stop. Don't leak the query handle.
- Per-core array length must match logical_cpus on Windows (verified to be correct already on the i5-1340P).

## Testing

Cannot be smoke-tested on macOS — only cross-compiles and ships as a Windows .exe. Verification path:
1. ./build --platform windows
2. scp to nuc13-002 (or any Windows NUC)
3. Run --duration 60s --json
4. Confirm frequency_series shows realistic values (1000-4400 MHz range for i5-1340P) and varies during the run

## Pairs with

- fleetbench-s3z (the existing freq sampler that left this hook explicitly)
- fleetbench-9wu (the --duration mode this depends on)
- fleetbench-jfc (separately tracked AVX/FMA torture workload — can stay deferred since this PDH work unblocks the *current* sustained-integer-load torture mode for Mark)

Promote priority to P1: this is now the blocker for delivering useful thermal-throttle evidence to Mark on Windows NUCs.
close_reason: PDH backend confirmed working on i5-1340P NUC. 11-sample 10s run showed per_core_mhz varying across samples (0-4257 MHz range), real boost/throttle behavior, not the flat [1900x8,1400x8] of the sysinfo backend. Polish commit 01f88ec adds 100ms prime sleep to fix t=0 zeros.

title: Add torture/stress CPU mode (time-bounded sustained load)
description:
Mark Cornmesser flagged that fleetbench's current cpu modes run too short to surface thermal throttling on Windows NUCs — even `long` (1B prime limit × 3 iter) completes well before the package heats into throttle. He uses prime95 torture mode (StressCPU.ps1) for this today.

Add a new time-bounded mode to the v0 cpu suite that loops the existing MT sieve workload until a wall-clock duration elapses, emitting per-iteration timings as a time series. Same workload as `normal`/`long` so it stays cross-platform and comparable; only the stopping condition changes.

Scope:
- New CLI flag (e.g. `--duration 10m`) or new mode preset (e.g. `torture` / `stress`). Probably a flag — orthogonal to mode.
- Loop sieve::run_mt iterations until elapsed >= duration, accumulate iteration records.
- Schema: extend Config with optional `duration_seconds`; results stay the same shape (iterations vector, just longer).
- Human output: print elapsed + iteration count.
- Not scheduled by the runner on every boot. Manual / out-of-band cadence only. Runner-side gating handled separately (or via existing --min-interval with a high value).

Pairs with the frequency-sampling bead — a long run without freq samples only shows throttling indirectly (iteration time drift). With samples, you see it directly.

Out of scope: prime95 shell-out on Windows. Different tool, different job (forensics vs baseline).
close_reason: Implemented --duration flag on cpu subcommand: time-bounded MT sieve loop, skips 1t to keep all cores hot, schema gains optional duration_seconds, iterations field reports actual count completed.

title: adb: env capture gaps on Linux (lsusb_topology empty, device fields null in adb_env)
description:
Smoke-test run on bitbar host (task NuqnawHXR0iJyOPmSZkSvA) exposed three env-block gaps in fleetbench adb output:

1. adb_env.lsusb_topology is empty string on Linux. This is the flagship hub-correlation field — without it, concurrent invocations cannot be correlated to specific USB hub positions, which is the entire point of capturing it. Likely causes to investigate: lsusb missing from $PATH on bitbar workers, shell-out failing silently, output captured to stdout vs stderr mix-up, or a code path that only runs when N>1 device. Test on a Linux box with lsusb installed and a phone attached locally to repro.

2. adb_env.device_serial and adb_env.device_model are null even though those same fields ARE present per-iteration on each entry in adb_results.iterations[]. So the data isn't being lost; the env-block summary is just not being populated. Likely a one-line oversight in the env builder.

3. host.os_release is null. Hostname is captured ('bitbar-ubuntu-157') but the OS release field is null. Lower priority — the cpu subcommand likely has the same behavior or has it working, worth comparing.

All three are diagnostic-affecting, not data-corrupting. The per-iteration data is fine. Fix is in the env-builder code path.

Repro: any fleetbench adb run on a Linux host emits this. Source artifact: task NuqnawHXR0iJyOPmSZkSvA, public/out/fleetbench-adb.json.

title: adb: incremental JSON output (stream per-iteration timings, not just final envelope)
description:
Today fleetbench adb writes its JSON envelope only when all iterations complete. If the process is killed mid-run (TC max-run-time hit, OOM, network hiccup, user ^C), all completed-iteration timing data is lost — stderr shows progress markers but no timings.

Concrete loss: task gsK18rDwR1eHM3uftfvGQA (LT TCP exploration) ran for 75s before TC's 90s maxRunTime killed it. It had completed 25B push x5, 25B pull x5, 1M push x2, 1M pull x2, 10M push 1/2 — all that timing data went in the bit bucket because the final envelope was never written. Re-running with a longer timeout is fine, but for ad-hoc exploration where you don't know how long things will take, losing in-progress data is rough.

What to add:
- Option (--ndjson-iterations, or always on alongside the envelope): emit one JSON line per completed iteration to stdout as they finish. Schema: {size_bytes, direction, iter_index, device_serial, elapsed_ms, bytes_per_sec, sha256_ok, timestamp}. At end-of-run, the existing single-object envelope still gets written.
- Caller can then `tee` or split the stream: line-delimited per-iter records into one file, the final envelope into another. Or just one file with the per-iter lines preceding the envelope.

Alternative shape: write the envelope incrementally to a --partial file (rename .partial -> final on clean exit; leave .partial behind on abort). The runner pattern already does this (filenames.py). Probably more consistent with the existing fleetbench style than ndjson streaming. Pick one in implementation.

Either way, the goal: a killed run leaves usable data behind.

Adjacent fix (worth checking in the same PR): tc_run_adb.py should `cat` the stderr log into the task log on failure paths so the operator can see *where* it died without downloading the artifact.

title: adb device file-copy benchmark mode (USB contention debugging)
description:
On hosts that have USB-attached Android devices (bitbar / LambdaTest clusters), characterize adb push/pull behavior to debug 'why is provisioning slow today?' style problems and compare vendors. Complements (does not replace) any in-tree raptor-side instrumentation.

Motivating signal: a 100-retrigger comparison of identical Speedometer 3 jobs across vendors (a55 hardware, Chrome-m, no-fission) showed LT push latency spanning 280-1600ms while BitBar held a tight 280-470ms. Means were misleading (LT mean *lower* than BitBar mean); the distribution width was the whole story.

Scope: a new top-level subcommand `fleetbench adb` that runs on the Linux Docker HOST where adb lives. Schema-compatible with the existing envelope (schema_version, host, env, config, results) so it flows through the same analysis pipeline.

## Design decisions (resolved)

- Subcommand: new top-level `fleetbench adb`. Do NOT shove I/O into the `cpu` subcommand.
- Production unit = one collector invocation, one device. Contention is observed by running many invocations concurrently at the TC layer, matching how real tests behave. No in-collector --parallel mode.
- Target selection: `--serial <id>` to pick a device; fail if multiple attached and no filter given.
- Remote path: default `/data/local/tmp/` (avoids FUSE on /sdcard, cleaner USB/adb signal). `--remote-path` flag to override (e.g. `/sdcard/Download` to reproduce raptor's path).
- Payload generation: pre-generate N distinct random files (one per iteration) before the timed section. Avoids page-cache reuse confounding bandwidth measurements. SHA256 verify round-trip (push → pull to different path → compare hashes).
- Bidirectional: time push and pull separately, both emit per-iteration timings.
- Sizes: 25 bytes (matches raptor's adb-latency probe — characterizes command/setup overhead, no bytes-on-wire), 1 MB, 10 MB, 100 MB. The 25-byte point is where the LT/BitBar variance gap actually showed up.
- Iterations: per-size, user-controlled (no global default). Sensible defaults baked in per size, e.g. `{25B: 200, 1MB: 100, 10MB: 30, 100MB: 10}` — avoids `--sizes 100M --iterations 200` footguns.
- Stats: collector emits raw per-iteration timings only. No median/IQR/summary — analysis layer handles that. Distribution is the signal, not the mean.
- adb dependency: capture `adb --version` in env block; accept `--adb-path` override (don't assume PATH).
- USB topology: capture `lsusb -t` output per device in env block on Linux. Windows topology punted (both vendors run Linux Docker for adb; not needed).

## Per-iteration output

device serial, device model, hub path (lsusb), file size, direction (push/pull), bytes/sec, elapsed_ms, sha256_ok

## Perfherder output

See [[fleetbench-perfherder-adapter]] — fleetbench-adb is the immediate motivating consumer. Matching the raptor adb-latency series (25-byte push to /sdcard/Download) is one of the comparability cases that adapter needs to handle.

## Not blocking

LambdaTest variance is the active pain point as of 2026-05; this lands when we want better data than the in-tree raptor-side instrumentation (which may or may not land) provides.
close_reason: Implemented and validated against real Android device (Pixel 10 Pro). Production deployment to bitbar/LT Linux Docker hosts is environmental, not code work.

comments.author: aerickson
comments.text: Implemented on branch aerickson/fleetbench-adb-io-bench-gjb (commit 44d1286). New 'fleetbench adb' subcommand with push/pull timed loops, pre-generated unique random payloads, SHA256 verification (remote sha256sum on push, local hash on pull), adb_version + lsusb -t env capture, schema v6 with adb_config/adb_env/adb_results siblings. README updated. 44/44 unit tests pass; smoke-tested on macOS dev box (no_device error path renders cleanly with adb --version captured). NOT closing: needs validation against a real device on a bitbar/LT-style Linux Docker host before close.

comments.author: aerickson
comments.text:
Validated end-to-end against a real Pixel 10 Pro on macOS dev box (collector 0.3.0+1415536). 21/21 iterations sha256_ok=true, status=ok, schema v6 envelope well-formed.

Per-size summary (n=5 / n=2 / n=2 / n=1):
- 25B    push 33-46ms,           pull 24-45ms             (command/setup overhead, no bytes on wire — the LT-vs-bitbar variance window)
- 1M     push 77-83ms (~13MB/s), pull 60-64ms (~17MB/s)
- 10M    push 360-402ms (~27MB/s), pull 316-340ms (~32MB/s)
- 100M   push 3050ms (~34MB/s),  pull 2707ms (~39MB/s)

Pull is consistently faster than push (known adb asymmetry). Throughput climbs with size as fixed overhead amortizes. Even at n=5 the 25B push tail is ~40% wider than the median, exactly the distribution shape the design called out.

Environmental specifics for the production target (Linux Docker host with bitbar/LT phones) — populated /proc-based env block, lsusb_topology capture — are code paths that already exist and run on Linux; not code work, just deployment validation when someone wires this into a TC task. Closing.

title: adb: --iterations doesn't restrict the size set; combined with --sizes is non-obvious
description:
fleetbench adb's --iterations flag is interpreted as 'override the iteration count for these sizes' rather than 'run only these sizes with these counts.' That means passing `--iterations 25B=5,1M=2,10M=2` (intending to skip 100M for a quick TCP probe) still runs 100M with its default iteration count of 10. To actually limit which sizes run, you must also pass `--sizes 25B,1M,10M`.

Concrete burn: task W6vxNvUkQamWaixY-P8FTw was set up to skip 100M for a TCP-over-LT smoke test (where 100M takes minutes per iteration). The 100M block ran anyway with default count=10 and the task hit TC's 10-minute maxRunTime mid-run, losing all data because incremental output isn't implemented yet ([[fleetbench-adb-incremental-output-vhm]]). User had to re-run with explicit --sizes.

This is a small UX gotcha that costs a real iteration loop when the run is expensive. Three plausible fixes (pick one):

1. Make --iterations imply --sizes (only run sizes listed in --iterations). Most intuitive: the flag does what you'd guess from its content. Breaks back-compat if anyone was relying on the override-only meaning, but that's a thin slice.
2. Error out if --iterations names a size that's not in the default size set OR not in --sizes; force the operator to be explicit. Safer; nag-louder behavior.
3. Just document the interaction loudly in README and --help text. Cheap; doesn't fix the footgun.

Recommendation: option 1 (make --iterations imply --sizes), with --sizes still working as an explicit override for the rare case where you want a size run at its default iteration count.

Stretch: also document in --help that the default size set is fixed (25B, 1M, 10M, 100M) so the operator knows what they're omitting if they use --sizes.

title: adb: capture device transport (usb/tcp) and add --transport filter
description:
On LambdaTest hosts, 'adb devices' returns both a USB serial and a network adb endpoint (e.g. R5CX23RT8WW + 10.146.6.230:5555). fleetbench adb today bails with 'multiple_devices' and requires --serial to disambiguate — but the bigger issue is that the two transports measure fundamentally different things. USB-attached adb measures the USB/hub/cable path; TCP-attached adb measures an IP network path layered on top. Comparing 'bitbar adb push' (USB) to 'LT adb push' (TCP) is apples-to-oranges by default.

Concrete failures observed:
- task feDAqOshQTSCB46FcoPeBA: status=failed, error.kind=multiple_devices (R5CX23RT8WW + 10.146.6.230:5555)
- task mXP_s1doSEuVZFVd4t3mRA: status=failed, error.kind=no_device — hardcoding --serial 10.146.6.230:5555 from the first task's host did not work on a different LT worker, because the network adb endpoint IP is per-host and TC schedules tasks across hosts. Hardcoded serials are structurally wrong for LT; --transport tcp is the right interface.

What to add:
1. Per-device transport classification in adb_env (and per-iteration if a single run somehow touches multiple). Heuristic: serial matching r'^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+:\d+$' (or ':\d+$') is TCP, otherwise USB. Capture as `transport: 'usb' | 'tcp'`.
2. New --transport flag {usb, tcp, any} with default 'any' for back-compat OR 'usb' for stricter measurement — discuss. Filters the device list before the multi-device check. With --transport tcp and exactly one TCP device present, fleetbench should pick it automatically without --serial.
3. Document in README that on hosts with mixed transports (LT specifically), the default behavior may surprise; recommend explicit --serial or --transport.

Stretch: capture `adb -s <serial> transport-id` and `adb -s <serial> features` in adb_env per device — they expose the underlying transport details (USB speed class, network address) that analysis would want.

Workaround currently in place: scripts/tc_run_adb.py does the TCP-device auto-pick in the wrapper (regex match on output of 'adb devices'). Should be removed once this lands.

Motivating evidence captured in [[fleetbench-adb-io-bench-gjb]] discussion: LT's wide push-latency distribution (280-1600ms vs bitbar's 280-470ms) may partly be IP-network noise on top of USB, not USB contention alone. Without transport capture we can't separate those signals.

comments.author: aerickson
comments.text: Nuance worth recording: TCP transport != WiFi. A network adb endpoint (ip:port) only means adbd is reached over an IP socket -- the far end may be the phone's own WiFi radio, OR a network tunnel to a different host that has the phone USB-attached locally (the likely shape in a device lab like LT). adb cannot distinguish these; the transport classification can only report usb vs tcp, not the physical link behind a tcp endpoint. Capturing wired-vs-wireless would need out-of-band lab config, not adb. Documented in docs/ADB_TESTING.md.

title: Bump warmup_prime_limit from 10^7 to 10^8
description: Smoke testing on Xeon E3-1585L v5 (slow x86 fleet host) showed iter 0 still ~20% slower than iters 1-2 in both 1t and mt paths, indicating the governor was still ramping after warmup. At 10^7 warmup completes in ~17ms on this class of host — not enough to fully ramp from idle. Bump WARMUP_PRIME_LIMIT to 10^8 (~170ms on slow x86, ~10ms on fast hosts) to bridge the full idle-to-load transition before timed runs.
close_reason: WARMUP_PRIME_LIMIT bumped from 10_000_000 to 100_000_000. On slow x86 hosts this gives ~170 ms of sustained CPU work to fully ramp the governor before timed runs; fast hosts trade <10 ms of warmup overhead for a known starting point. Smoke retest on t-linux64-ms-005 pending.

title: Refactor env sampling: raw /proc/stat snapshots instead of computed cpu_percent
description:
Current cpu_percent computation in env.rs sleeps 100ms between two /proc/stat reads. Done three times per cpu run (pre-warmup, pre-timed, post-timed), this 300ms of idle time lets the CPU governor down-clock — observable as a consistent ~17% iter-0 penalty in prime_sieve_1t at normal mode on Xeon E3-1585L v5 even with the 10^8 warmup bump.

Fix: emit raw cpu time counters at each sample point. No sleep. Analysis layer differences any two snapshots to compute CPU% over any window (warmup window, timed window, or subsets).

Schema change: LoadSample.cpu_percent -> LoadSample.cpu_counters { idle_units, iowait_units, total_units, kind }. Bumps schema_version 2 -> 3. Update design v2 doc to reflect new shape.
close_reason: LoadSample.cpu_percent -> LoadSample.cpu_counters (idle_units, iowait_units, total_units, kind). Single /proc/stat read, no sleep, no governor down-clock. Schema bumped 2 -> 3. Design v2 doc updated to reflect the new shape and the rationale (raw-data-first, no in-collector rate computation). Smoke validator updated. 29 tests pass.

description: Deterministic FP/vector loop (dot product or small matmul). Single thread. Correctness checked with tolerance, not exact equality. Measures FP/SIMD/FMA throughput.

title: stability_loop workload + summary-stats decision
description: Run a short workload repeatedly, emit all timings. Measures variance, thermal ramp-down, noisy neighbors. Decide here whether median/cov summary belongs in collector output for this specific workload (the v0 'no summary stats' rule may have one exception).

title: Preserve cpu-v0 suite behavior alongside cpu-v1
description: cpu_suite_version selectable. v0 results remain bit-for-bit reproducible after v1 lands. v1 is additive, not a rename.

title: Add a time-targeted mode (pick prime_limit to hit ~N ms wall time)
description:
Current modes are fixed-limit: quick=10^7, normal=10^8, long=10^9. Per-iteration wall time therefore varies dramatically by hardware class (180ms on Xeon E3, 90ms on M4 Pro, 250ms on Pixel 10 Pro for normal). Below ~100ms/iter signal quality degrades on the fast end of the fleet.

A time-targeted mode would auto-pick prime_limit to hit a target per-iteration wall time (~500ms). Each host gets the same statistical signal quality regardless of speed.

Tradeoffs:
- Breaks determinism: prime_limit varies per host, so cross-host comparisons of seconds-per-iteration become apples-to-oranges. Comparable metric becomes work-per-second instead.
- Requires a calibration run to pick the limit.
- Schema needs a way to capture work-units-completed alongside seconds, or analysis has to back-compute it.

Listed as an open question in design v2. Worth doing once the fleet shows both Xeon-class and M-class hardware needing good outlier detection from the same suite.

title: Add fp_vector_mt AVX/FMA torture workload to match prime95 thermal envelope
description:
The integer sieve under --duration (fleetbench-9wu) will surface gross thermal problems — degraded TIM, dead fan, etc. — under sustained 100% load, but it won't reliably reproduce the AVX-offset throttling that only appears under FMA-heavy workloads. Prime95's Small FFTs is specifically tuned to keep cores compute-bound and cache-resident on the widest execution units; integer code with memory traffic lets cores idle on RAM, so package power and core temps undershoot what prime95 produces.

Add a multi-threaded FMA-heavy workload:
- Per-thread cache-resident FP buffer (L1/L2-sized) so cores stay compute-bound.
- Tight FMA loop on the widest available vector width.
- Runs under --duration alongside the integer sieve and emits per-iteration timings (same shape as prime_sieve_mt).
- Tolerance-based correctness check (FP results are non-deterministic across cores/runs).
- Pairs with the existing freq sampler (fleetbench-s3z) so frequency decay shows up in frequency_series alongside any AVX-offset behavior.

Distinct from fleetbench-cpu-suite-v1-w1q.3 (fp_vector_1t), which targets throughput measurement on a single core. Different goals: throughput baseline vs. thermal worst-case. They could share a kernel later if scope allows, but keeping them separate avoids muddying either signal.

## Implementation notes (point 2)

Doing this well in Rust is non-trivial:
- Cannot trust compiler auto-vectorization to reliably emit AVX2/FMA. Need explicit `#[target_feature(enable = "avx2,fma")]` with intrinsics on x86_64, and NEON intrinsics on aarch64, with a scalar fallback path.
- Adding a SIMD-helper dependency (`wide`, `pulp`, or similar) is acceptable if it cuts implementation time substantially — the project is OK with adding deps when they save real work. Evaluate at start of work: hand-rolled intrinsics vs. crate, pick whichever is less code with comparable thermal output.
- Verify with a microbenchmark + `perf stat` (Linux) or VTune/Intel SDE that the inner loop is actually issuing FMA instructions and saturating the vector units before integrating.

## Why this is delayed (point 1)

We don't yet have data on whether the integer-sieve torture mode is already "good enough" for Mark's actual use case (debugging Windows NUC thermal throttling). NUCs with real hardware problems will throttle under any sustained 100% load. Ship fleetbench-9wu + fleetbench-s3z first, get Windows envelopes back from the fleet, and only build this if integer-load freq_series demonstrably undershoots the throttling Mark sees with his prime95-based StressCPU.ps1. Don't build speculatively.

## Reuse (point 3)

Gated on real-world data from fleetbench-9wu/s3z. When built, this workload runs under the same --duration plumbing and emits into the same frequency_series we already added, so the torture-mode infrastructure pays off twice.

title: Decide: CPython available on Windows perf hosts?
description: If yes, runner is Python. If no, ship as PyInstaller frozen exe or port runner to Rust. Gates runner language choice. Open question from design v2.

title: Perfherder output adapter (--perfherder flag)
description:
Add an opt-in output mode that emits Perfherder-compatible JSON alongside the native envelope. Applies to all subcommands (cpu, adb, future suites) — not specific to one workload.

Why: when fleetbench runs under Taskcluster, Perfherder solves visualization, cross-pool comparison, alerting, and historical trending for free. The native envelope remains the source of truth (raw, full metadata, downstream analysis pipeline); the Perfherder line is a rendered view for the TC log parser.

Trigger: looking at a side-by-side adb-push-latency series, the mean was actively misleading (LT mean 260ms 'beat' BitBar mean 327ms), but the replicates view showed LT spans 200-1600ms vs BitBar's tight 200-400ms cluster. Perfherder's replicates view is the right visualization and we don't have to build it.

Shape:
- New global flag --perfherder (or per-subcommand) that, when set, emits an additional 'PERFHERDER_DATA: {...}' line on stdout that TC's log parser picks up.
- Native envelope still emitted on stdout as today; perfherder is additive, not a replacement.
- Schema reference: perfherder-data.json — framework + suites[] with subtests[], value, replicates[], lowerIsBetter, unit.
- Per-subcommand mapping: each subcommand decides which raw timings become the perfherder 'value' (usually median) and which go in 'replicates'. Keep the mapping in the subcommand module, not in a shared layer — the suites differ enough that abstraction would hurt.

Notes / open questions:
- Framework name: register 'fleetbench' as a perfherder framework, or piggyback on an existing one? Needs a sign-off from perf team.
- Suite/subtest naming convention: 'fleetbench-cpu' suite with subtests per workload (sieve_1t, sieve_mt); 'fleetbench-adb' suite with subtests per (size, direction). Document the naming so dashboards stay stable across schema versions.
- When --duration (torture mode) is active, the perfherder 'value' is ambiguous — emit frequency_series summary stats instead of throughput? Probably skip perfherder output for duration runs in v0 and revisit.

Not blocking. Becomes useful the moment fleetbench runs under TC against the bitbar/LT pools — at which point this is the cheapest way to get a usable dashboard.

Related: [[fleetbench-adb-io-bench-gjb]] is the immediate motivating consumer; the cpu suite would benefit too.

title: Decide: latest.json symlink/copy in results dir
description: Convenient for local inspection but adds a write-ordering concern. Open question from design v2.

title: Decide: redundant runner-side load sample

close_reason: Moot: env sampling now emits raw counter snapshots (fleetbench-collector-v0-8ne.14), so there is no duplicate-sample concern between runner and collector.

title: Decide: record scheduling source in envelope
description: Envelope could record systemd unit name / cron line / scheduled task name when discoverable. Useful for debugging missed runs.
close_reason: Moot: trigger is boot/manual under the new operational model; there is no external scheduler unit name to discover.

title: Add GitHub Actions release workflow to publish per-platform binaries
description:
On 'v*' tag push, build all four platform binaries and publish them to a GitHub release.

Workflow shape (rough):
- Trigger: push to a tag matching v*
- Jobs (matrix):
  - ubuntu-latest: cargo zigbuild --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl AND x86_64-pc-windows-gnu (one runner does both via zigbuild)
  - macos-latest: cargo build --release --target aarch64-apple-darwin (native Apple toolchain)
  - ubuntu-latest with android-actions/setup-android: cargo ndk -t aarch64-linux-android -- build --release
- After matrix completes: collect all four binaries, compute SHA256SUMS, upload to the GitHub release via softprops/action-gh-release or equivalent

Naming convention (already documented in README Distribution section):
  fleetbench-<version>-linux-x86_64
  fleetbench-<version>-windows-x86_64.exe
  fleetbench-<version>-macos-aarch64
  fleetbench-<version>-android-aarch64
  SHA256SUMS

Considerations:
- Cargo.toml version should match the tag (workflow can verify or fail loudly)
- Decide: should release also tag the runner version, or is the collector versioned independently?
- Decide: include source tarball? .deb/.rpm packaging? Probably no for v0 — single binaries are sufficient.
- TC fetches typically prefer raw binaries with sha256 pinning, not archive bundles

Not blocking any current work. Lift to in_progress when fleet integration actually needs versioned releases.
close_reason: Shipped. .github/workflows/release.yml builds linux-musl, windows-gnu, macos-aarch64, android-aarch64 on v* tag push, computes SHA256SUMS, publishes a release via softprops/action-gh-release. v0.1.0 dry-run on aerickson/fleetbench succeeded; v0.2.0 cut as first official release on origin.

title: Python runner
description: Milestone 2: runner that wraps the collector and persists results. Operational model: invoked by the worker-startup wrapper before the TC worker boots; self-throttles based on the newest envelope timestamp in the results dir (no separate state). Linux-first; Windows deferred until m2-cpython-windows is answered. Reboot-per-test means many invocations per day — most exit fast as no-ops once --min-interval is satisfied.
close_reason: Shipped: collector v0.2.0 with cpu-v0 suite, Linux runner complete. Windows follow-ups (.5, .8) detached and tracked standalone.

title: Scaffold runner/ package
description: Create runner/ directory with package layout, entry point fleetbench-run. Language decided by m2-cpython-windows question.
close_reason: Runner scaffolded as a uv-managed Python package. src/fleetbench_run/ layout with console_scripts entry point fleetbench-run. CLI skeleton in cli.py owns argparse for --results-dir, --mode, --collector-binary, --min-interval, --skip-activity-check, --trigger, --timeout — flags match design v2. main() stub returns 1 with a 'not yet implemented' message. 6 unit tests cover help rendering, required args, defaults, all-flags parse, and rejection of bad enum values. uv sync + uv run pytest green.

title: Throttle check: derive last-run from results dir
description: On startup, list results dir and find the newest envelope filename. Parse its embedded UTC timestamp and compare to now() minus --min-interval. If the interval is not yet satisfied, log 'last run was Xh ago, skipping' and exit 0. Otherwise proceed with the run. Counts any envelope file (success or failure) as a run, to avoid burning every reboot retrying on a degraded host. No separate sentinel file — results dir is the single source of truth.
close_reason: throttle.decide(now, results_dir, min_interval) returns ThrottleDecision(should_run, reason, last_run_utc). find_latest_envelope_time reads only filenames (no file opens), skips .partial and any non-envelope-shaped name, returns None for empty or missing dir. Boundary is inclusive: elapsed == min_interval runs. Zero interval always runs. Human-friendly duration formatting (1d1h, 12h, 30s) appears in the reason strings so logs read naturally. 13 tests cover empty/missing dir, multiple envelopes, partial-file exclusion, garbage tolerance, runs/skips on both sides of the boundary, zero interval, exact boundary, naive-datetime rejection.

title: Activity pre-flight via gwhc (Linux)
description: Before invoking the collector, query gwhc --json on Linux hosts. If state != IDLE, log the gwhc summary (state, state_description, any non-passing checks, warnings) and exit 0. Defense in depth: the operational model already runs the runner pre-worker-startup, but a manual invocation mid-test would otherwise produce noisy results. Skippable via --skip-activity-check. Non-Linux hosts skip the check silently (gwhc is Linux-only).
close_reason: activity.check_activity() runs gwhc --json with a 10s timeout, parses state, blocks the run when state != IDLE. Missing gwhc, non-JSON output, non-object JSON, and missing 'state' field all handled distinctly: gwhc-absent and non-parseable output are treated as advisory (proceed); missing 'state' in valid JSON blocks (better to skip than record noisy data). Invoker is dependency-injected so all 8 tests are pure unit tests with stubbed gwhc output. cli.main() runs the check between throttle and perform_run; --skip-activity-check bypasses entirely. E2E verified on macOS (gwhc absent → silent proceed) and via --skip-activity-check (no check line printed).

title: CLI: --min-interval with duration parsing
description: Parse human-friendly durations on the --min-interval flag: 30m, 1h, 24h, 7d, etc. Reject ambiguous units. Convert internally to a timedelta. Default value: 24h. Used by the throttle check.
close_reason: parse_duration() in fleetbench_run.duration accepts <integer><s|m|h|d> and returns a timedelta. Compound forms, fractional values, bare numbers, unsupported units, and negatives are rejected with a clear message. Zero is allowed (run every invocation). Wired into argparse via type= so bad values on --min-interval or --timeout fail at parse time with the same descriptive error. 10 new duration tests; 26 total green.

title: Update design v2 doc: boot-throttle operational model
description: Rewrite the runner section of docs/fleetbench_design_v2.md to reflect the new operational model: invoked by worker-startup wrapper before TC worker boot, self-throttles based on newest envelope timestamp, gwhc pre-flight, --min-interval CLI arg. Remove the systemd-timer / Task Scheduler examples. Note that --min-interval is a soft lower bound dependent on reboot frequency. Multiple-mode-per-host (different cadences per mode) explicitly listed as future v0.x work.
close_reason: Design v2 runner section rewritten to reflect the boot-throttle operational model. Replaced the systemd-timer/Task-Scheduler scheduling section with Operational Model, Throttle Decision, and Activity Pre-flight sections. Envelope shape updated: trigger now boot|manual, run_id is 32-char uuid4 hex (not ULID), scheduled_for_utc field removed, collector_killed_by_runner shown. CLI options updated with --min-interval, --skip-activity-check, --timeout and notes on duration parsing. Open Questions pruned of items that are no longer applicable (load_sample duplication, scheduling source); added per-mode cadence as deferred future work. M2 milestone bullets updated to match what shipped.

title: Subprocess invocation + stdout capture
description: Shell out to collector with configured --mode and --json. Capture stdout, stderr, exit code. Do not parse or transform the collector results block.
close_reason: collector.run_collector() invokes the binary with 'cpu --mode <mode> --json', captures stdout/stderr/exit_code, and returns a frozen CollectorResult dataclass with started_utc/finished_utc bookends. Timeout argument is honored: on subprocess.TimeoutExpired the child is killed (single-process kill only for now; .7 will swap in process-group SIGKILL), partial stdout/stderr is preserved, and killed_by_timeout=True is set in the result. FileNotFoundError propagates so the orchestrator (in .6) can wrap it into a failure envelope. 5 tests cover happy-path output capture, non-zero exit propagation, timeout-kill behavior, exact invocation argv, and missing-binary error.

title: Envelope format (run_id ULID, trigger, timing, exit code)
description: Envelope wraps collector JSON unmodified. Fields: envelope_version, runner_version, run_id (ULID), trigger ('boot' or 'manual'), started_utc, finished_utc, collector_exit_code, collector_output. Collector output preserved bit-for-bit. 'boot' indicates the runner was invoked from the worker-startup wrapper; 'manual' is for ad-hoc operator runs.
close_reason: envelope.py defines the frozen Envelope dataclass and build_envelope() factory. Success path: parsed_output populates collector_output; the three diagnostic fields stay None and are omitted from JSON. Failure path: collector_output=null, stdout_raw/stderr/parse_error populated, with both raw streams truncated to 16 KB on a UTF-8 boundary so multi-byte chars aren't split. CollectorResult timestamps and killed_by_timeout propagate. envelope_to_json drops failure fields on success and keeps them (even when null) on failure so consumers can tell 'parsed but empty' from 'never relevant'. Bit-for-bit preservation of collector JSON is asserted. 12 new tests; 70 total.

title: Atomic write: .partial + os.replace
description: Write envelope to <name>.json.partial, fsync, then atomically rename to <name>.json. Use os.replace (works on Windows; overwrites atomically). Collection tool can safely skip *.partial.
close_reason: disk.write_envelope and disk.write_text_atomically implement the .partial+rename discipline. Steps: write to sibling .json.partial, fsync the file, os.replace into final name, then fsync the containing directory on POSIX (silently skipped on Windows). Errors mid-write cleanup the partial. Pre-existing partials from prior crashes are overwritten by the next run with the same filename (highly unlikely given uuid4 run_ids but covered). os.replace gives atomic overwrite on both POSIX and Windows. 8 tests cover dir creation, content correctness, no-leftover partials, atomic replacement, stale-partial recovery, partial-cleanup-on-error, and the partial-path discipline.

title: Filename scheme
description: <ts>_<host>_<suite>_<run_id>.json. ISO-8601 UTC with : replaced by - (Windows legal). Sortable, globbable, no appended files.
close_reason: filenames.py owns the envelope filename contract. make_envelope_filename produces <ts>_<host>_<suite>_<run_id>.json with Windows-legal characters (no colons), UTC normalization for non-UTC inputs, hostname/suite sanitization to [A-Za-z0-9-], and rejection of naive datetimes. partial_path_for and is_partial / is_final_envelope handle the .partial discipline. parse_started_utc round-trips the timestamp out of a filename and powers the throttle check landing in .10. generate_run_id returns 32-char hex uuid4. 14 tests cover shape, Windows-safety, UTC normalization, sanitization, round-trip parsing, partial detection, sort order, and run-id format.

title: Hard-failure handling: non-JSON, panic, stderr capture
description: On non-JSON stdout / parse error / panic / signal kill: still write envelope with collector_output=null, collector_stdout_raw, collector_stderr (both 16 KB cap), collector_output_parse_error, collector_killed_by_runner=false. Runner exits 0; benchmark failure visible inside envelope.
close_reason: orchestrate.perform_run() wires collector + parse + envelope + disk into one flow. parse_collector_output enforces 'stdout must be a single JSON object'; empty stdout, syntax errors, arrays, and scalars all become structured parse_error messages. Hard failures — non-JSON stdout, missing binary (FileNotFoundError), timeout kills — all produce a failure envelope on disk and the runner exits 0; the collector's status is preserved inside the envelope. On parse failure the filename's suite slot falls back to 'unknown-suite' so contaminated runs are visibly distinct from clean ones. cli.main() now performs the throttle check, calls perform_run when due, and prints which file was written. End-to-end smoke against the real collector confirms a 2.3 KB envelope lands correctly. 11 new tests; 89 total.

title: Timeout backstop + Linux process group SIGKILL
description: Default 10-minute hard timeout. Launch collector with os.setsid; on timeout send SIGKILL to process group. Set collector_killed_by_runner=true in envelope.
close_reason: collector.run_collector now uses Popen with preexec_fn=os.setsid on POSIX so the child becomes the leader of a new session/process group. On timeout, os.killpg(proc.pid, SIGKILL) reaps the entire group; any spawned descendants die along with the direct child. Windows falls back to single-process Popen.kill() pending the Job Object work (deferred to .8). Killed_by_timeout flag preserved. Drain-after-kill picks up any final buffered output. New test spawns a sleep grandchild from the fake collector and confirms (via os.kill(pid, 0)) that the grandchild is reaped after the runner timeout fires. 98 total tests green.

title: Windows Job Object (KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE)
description: Launch collector inside a Job Object with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE. On timeout close the job to kill collector + any descendants atomically. pywin32 or small ctypes wrapper. Set up from day one even though v0 spawns no children.

title: Scheduling docs: systemd timer + Task Scheduler
description: Document example systemd timer unit (Linux) and Windows Task Scheduler XML / schtasks command. Weekly cadence initial target. Runner itself is one-shot; OS does scheduling.

title: Sample CPU frequency periodically during cpu runs
description:
To detect thermal throttling from fleetbench data, we need per-sample CPU frequency over the duration of a run, not just aggregate iteration times. Currently the envelope captures load_pre_warmup / load_pre_timed / load_post_timed only.

Periodically sample CPU frequency (and current load) during the timed workload, push samples into the envelope as a time series. With a 10-min torture run, freq samples that drop from boost-clock to base-clock midway are the smoking gun for thermal throttle.

Scope:
- Background sampler thread, ~1Hz, started when timed workload begins, stopped when it ends.
- Cross-platform via sysinfo (per-core MHz). Windows accuracy can be improved later via PDH `\Processor Information(*)\Processor Frequency` if sysinfo proves insufficient.
- Schema: new optional Environment.frequency_samples (or env_series): [{t_offset_s, per_core_mhz: [...], load_pct: ...}]. Keep it bounded — 10 min @ 1Hz = 600 samples, fine for JSON envelope size.
- Only emit when the timed/torture mode is in use. Normal short runs don't need it.

Pairs with the torture-mode bead. Independently useful but most valuable in combination.
close_reason: Implemented background freq sampler at ~1Hz during --duration runs. New FrequencySample schema (t_offset_seconds, per_core_mhz, mean_mhz); Output gains optional frequency_series. SCHEMA_VERSION bumped 3->4. macOS placeholder values documented; Linux/Windows return real per-core MHz.
